summary: A first-person essay on experiencing virtual reality art, centered on the 'VirtuArt' showcase in September 2023 and conversations with VR artists. The author argues that VR is a paradigm shift because it makes art immersive, interactive, multisensory and more accessible, letting audiences step into the artwork. Artists Jacob Torres and Sophia Langley are quoted on emotion and memory in VR.
one_line: A personal essay on how immersive, interactive VR art, seen at the 2023 'VirtuArt' showcase, changes how audiences experience and access art.
key_facts: The author attended the 'VirtuArt' VR showcase on the evening of September 8, 2023.
'VirtuArt' was curated by VR artists including Emily O’Neil and Jacob Torres.
Emily O’Neil created an abstract cosmos platform where colors and shapes morphed in response to the author's movements.
One segment of the experience was an 'ocean of grief' painted in deep blue hues with sorrowful strings.
On October 15, 2023, the author spoke with Jacob Torres, whose VR exhibition was titled 'Synthesis of Awe'.
Jacob Torres said VR lets you stand in an artist's emotion and feel the atmosphere shift around you.
In VR art, interaction is required rather than forbidden, unlike the 'do not touch' policy in traditional museums.
Reaching toward a shimmering light triggered a symphony of illumination and sound, and each visitor had a unique experience.
Emergent VR artist Sophia Langley's piece, experienced on November 20, 2023, included a warm, sweet scent matching visual sunsets and virtual grass sensations.
Sophia Langley said memories created in VR 'are as potent as any other.'
The author argues VR democratizes art because anyone with VR access can visit worlds by skilled artists regardless of location.
VR has enabled artists from fields like game design and psychology to collaborate and influence art.
The author says there is no physical limitation to the size or scope of art in the digital realm.
